newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek Jews to claim Nazi-era gold from Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: Greek Jews to claim Nazi-era gold from Swiss banks.

text.p: Greek Jews said the publication of Holocaust-era accounts by Swiss banks could open the way for claiming 1.7 million gold sovereigns they paid the Nazis as ransom to save Jewish lives.
"This move opens the way for pushing our claims. We know a lot of this gold reached Swiss banks," Nissim Mais, president of the central board of the Jewish Community of Greece, told Reuters.

Greece's Jewish community, which was nearly exterminated by the Nazis, had yet to identify any of its members among the 14 Greek names on the list of more than 2,000 foreigners who held accounts in Switzerland before World War Two.
"No one has come forth yet to claim relation to any of the names but we are still waiting. Whatever happens, the fact that the accounts were opened is a moral victory," Mais said.

The Swiss Bankers Association advertised the list of pre-1945 accounts in newspapers in 28 countries. The dormant accounts are thought to be worth around 60 million Swiss francs ($40 million) -- much more than originally believed.

Mais said the move was bound to help claims by Greek Jews, helped by the World Jewish Congress, to recover their gold. He said the issue would be pushed either through Greek authorities or put directly to the Swiss banks.

About 54,000 Greek Jews were killed in the gas chambers of Auschwitz and Birkenau during the 1941-1944 Nazi occupation of Greece. Just a few thousand remain from a community numbering 80,000 at the turn of the century.

"Jewish community leaders were asked to gather gold sovereigns to hand as ransom to the Nazis in exchange for people's lives or for better treatment," Mais said. "We know that a big part of this gold was deposited by the Nazis in Swiss banks."
He said the Nazis used the same system in Italy, where they promised better treatment to extort Jewish wealth and then promptly wiped out the Jewish communities.
Most of the Greek gold was taken from the northern city of Salonika, known as Second Jerusalem for its prosperous large Jewish community.
Salonika's Jewish history stretches back to the second century BC and St Paul is known to have preached at its synagogue. Now the city has a dwindling community of about 1,000 Jews.
